subject: Banking
title: Payday Loans: Legal Loan Sharking
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Payday Loans: Legal Loan Sharking.

hook.text: Payday loans charge $15-30 per $100 borrowed for two weeks. That equals an annual rate of 400-780%. Legal loan sharking.

buildup.text: 12 million Americans use payday loans annually. The average borrower takes 8 loans per year.

discovery.text: Payday lenders cluster in low-income and minority neighborhoods.

twist.text: 80% of payday loans are rolled over into new loans. The borrower never pays off the principal, just the fees.

climax.text: Payday lending is a $9 billion industry built on trapping poor people in cycles of debt.

punchline.text: 400-780% APR. More shops than McDonald's. Legal debt traps for the poor.

quiz.question: What is the effective annual interest rate on payday loans?

details.summary: Payday loans are small, short-term loans typically due on the borrower's next payday, charging fees that translate to annual percentage rates of 300 to 500 percent. They target low-income borrowers who lack access to cheaper credit alternatives.
details.whyItMatters: Payday loans create a debt trap where borrowers repeatedly roll over loans because they cannot afford both the repayment and their living expenses. This cycle extracts billions from the poorest communities while providing temporary relief.
takeaways: Typical payday loan fees translate to 300 to 500 percent annual interest
Over 80 percent of payday loans are rolled over or followed by another loan
The industry generates over 9 billion dollars annually in fees from borrowers

faq.question: Why do people use payday loans if the rates are so high?
faq.answer: Desperation. When you face an emergency expense with no savings, poor credit, and no family support, a payday loan may be the only option available. The short-term need feels more urgent than the long-term cost.

faq.question: Are there better alternatives to payday loans?
faq.answer: Paycheck advance apps, credit union payday alternative loans, employer-sponsored emergency funds, and community assistance programs all offer cheaper options. Some charge small fees rather than triple-digit interest rates.
